deep.reconstruction: This page contains no mathematics. It holds personal and philosophical notes, probably written about 1938. (1) A planned title for a future book: 'Philosophie auf naturwissenschaftlicher Grundlage' (Philosophy on a natural-scientific foundation). The word 'künftigen' (future) is inserted above the line. (2) A characterization of 'today's worldview' through slogans: the 'political university'; science is not free of presuppositions but oriented on a 'völkisch' basis; antisemitism. Hilbert is recording the Nazi-era ideology of science. Given his known stance, this reads as a critical observation, but the page itself gives no explicit evaluation. (3) A note numbered '2': 'Only now, 20 years after the end of the war, do we become fully aware of what we lost through the war: Wolf, Behrens, Garbe!' With the end of the war in 1918, this dates the entry to about 1938. The three names are presumably young Göttingen scientists, possibly Hilbert's students or assistants, killed in World War I. Wolf and Garbe are underlined. I have not verified the identities. (4) A charade (Silbenrätsel) sent to Hilbert by a 'Müller' on 31 Dec 1902. In outline: when the first syllable 'falls from the hearts', we are always delighted; the second syllable has always been fought over with war-cries, not jests; may your neighbour [at table, or wife] never resemble the whole; may she show herself in the new year always young, beautiful and cheerful. The solution is not given on the page. The whole is evidently something old, ugly or sour, the opposite of 'young, beautiful, cheerful'. The first syllable plausibly relates to the idiom 'ein Stein/eine Last fällt vom Herzen'. I do not attempt a firm solution. (5) 'verte' (turn over). The previous page contains physics notes (a cohesion force) and ODE notes (the Hermite equation y''-2xy'+2ny=0 and its eigenvalue transformation), but none of that appears on this folio.
